55	
56	On MATH Level~4--5~\citep{math-2021} ($N{=}795$ problems, code interpreter as deterministic modality), internal reasoning and code interpretation achieve near-identical accuracy: $73.5\%$ vs.\ $73.0\%$ ($+0.5$~pp, McNemar $p = 0.81$, 95\% CI $[-2.6, +3.6]$~pp). The McNemar test compares binary correctness: 80 problems are solved only by internal reasoning and 76 only by code, yielding near-symmetric discordance ($\chi^2 = 0.10$). The label distribution is balanced: 107 \texttt{int\_preferred} vs.\ 95 \texttt{det\_preferred}, with 74.6\% \texttt{no\_preference}. The confirmed null rules out any routing signal of magnitude ${\geq}3.6$~pp at $\alpha{=}0.05$. The absence of systematic routing signal confirms that without catastrophic failure, modality routing confers no advantage in this domain.
57	
58	\subsection{Cross-Environment Contrasts}
59	\label{sec:cross-env}
60	
61	We evaluate two additional environments lacking catastrophic death penalties.
62	
63	\paragraph{ALFWorld.} ALFWorld~\citep{alfworld-2021} is a text-based household environment (6 task types, 135 games, max 50 steps). The two modalities differ in \emph{information access}: the deterministic strategy additionally receives admissible actions (an information asymmetry rather than a computation mode switch). The success rate gap is 27.4\% vs.\ 3.0\%, with 35 deterministic-preferred, 2 internal-preferred, and 98 no-preference labels (96 both-fail). The deterministic advantage stems from the information gap rather than death avoidance, a qualitatively different mechanism that the framework diagnoses without modification.
64	
65	\begin{table}[t]
66	\centering
67	\small
68	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
69	\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccc@{}}
70	\toprule
71	Environment & $N$ & Det\% & Int\% & NoPref\% & Death? \\
72	\midrule
73	ScienceWorld & 245 & 35.1 & 3.7 & 61.2 & Yes ($-100$) \\
74	MATH & 795 & 12.0 & 13.5 & 74.6 & No \\
75	ALFWorld & 135 & 25.9 & 1.5 & 72.6 & No\textsuperscript{$\dagger$} \\
76	\bottomrule
77	\end{tabular}}
78	\caption{Cross-environment label distribution. ScienceWorld exhibits strong deterministic preference driven by death avoidance; MATH shows balanced labels (no routing signal); ALFWorld shows deterministic preference driven by information asymmetry. $\dagger$\,ALFWorld's deterministic advantage stems from action-space pruning, not death avoidance.}
79	\label{tab:cross-env}
80	\end{table}
81	
82	\begin{figure}[t]
83	\centering
84	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/signal_reversal.pdf}

```text
107	\subsection{Router Training as Diagnostic Probe}
108	\label{sec:router-diagnostic}
109	
110	We probe whether counterfactual labels can train a step-level router, as a diagnostic of label informativeness. Two factors bound performance: the oracle margin is only 2.89 points ($-6.58$ vs.\ $-9.47$), capping routing upside; additionally, ${\sim}27.7\%$ of step-level labels are misaligned with their episode-level assignment (a secondary confound). An implicit router (Qwen3, LoRA fine-tuned; Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}) is trained at three scales (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B) with identical 4-seed configurations. Step-level balanced accuracy is flat across scales ($56.4 \pm 3.5\%$, $58.2 \pm 4.0\%$, $59.2 \pm 3.5\%$; all within seed variance); step-level discrimination is not capacity-sensitive. At episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline ($59.0 \pm 1.9\%$, $p < 0.005$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablations}), while 0.6B ($50.7 \pm 2.6\%$) and 1.7B ($43.1 \pm 1.0\%$) remain at or below chance. The 1.7B dip is robust across seeds (range $41.7$--$44.4\%$). We hypothesize that the 1.7B model has sufficient capacity to memorize death-correlated patterns in the training set but insufficient capacity to learn a generalizable routing policy, resulting in spurious anti-correlation; future work should examine per-class routing decisions to test this hypothesis. This non-monotonic pattern, combined with universally low internal recall, reinforces that learned routing does not scale predictably with capacity at current data scales.
111	
112	\paragraph{Augmentation scaling.} Augmentation-based scaling ($25\%$--$800\%$) via paraphrase provides no improvement (Appendix~\ref{app:seed-robustness}): paraphrase augmentation inflates the majority class (89.6\%$\rightarrow$97.7\%) without increasing minority-class diversity or generating novel routing patterns; real-data scaling (requiring ${\sim}1{,}350$ episode pairs for 50 minority-class examples) remains an open question. Capacity scaling improves episode-level routing ($+9$\,pp at 4B) without improving step-level accuracy (flat ${\sim}57\%$); the extractable signal is task-type-level structure.
113	
114	\paragraph{End-to-end deployment.} We deploy the best router (4B) in the full ScienceWorld loop ($N{=}245$ episodes, same task set as baselines) to test whether improved episode-level accuracy translates to deployment gains. The 4B router scores $-12.03$ (95\% CI: $[-17.82, -6.45]$), not exceeding always-deterministic ($-9.47$; overlapping CIs). The 1.7B router ($-10.70$; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}) performs comparably. Despite improved episode-level accuracy ($+9$\,pp at 4B), deployment score remains flat. The agent improvement results (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}) reinforce this ceiling: even Reflexion-level intervention leaves a 15.1~pp death gap to deterministic. Label quality is verified in Appendix~\ref{app:labeling}.
115	
116	Failure mode and ablation details in Appendices~\ref{app:failure-modes}--\ref{app:ablations}.
117	
```

<details><summary>↩ Tool result · `toolu_01RnwPnH9TKwEoNFtwRtRwGt`</summary>

```text
1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Why the router fails: task-type-level signal.}
5	The router diagnostic (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}) reveals a structural mismatch: death avoidance is a task-type-level binary property (10 of 11 types carry death risk), but step-level features correlate weakly with this signal because death risk depends on multi-step state trajectories, not individual action semantics. The 4B router's episode-level improvement ($59.0\%$) without step-level gains ($56$--$59\%$, flat) confirms that capacity scaling captures task-type classification rather than generalizable routing features.
6	
7	\paragraph{Non-triviality of death dominance.}
8	Three lines of evidence argue that death avoidance is not a trivially remediable artifact. First, scaling from 7B to 72B does not reduce death rates (preliminary 4/11 tasks: e.g., \texttt{chemistry-mix} 50\% at both scales). Second, retry without self-correction (44.5\%) does not improve over single-trial baseline (42.9\%): brute-force repetition cannot overcome structural state hallucination. Third, the effect is not uniform: \texttt{find-non-living-thing} exhibits 0\% death across all conditions, confirming that death risk is task-specific, not a blanket model deficiency. Only targeted cognitive intervention (Reflexion self-correction) partially reduces death from 42.9\% to 31.4\%, and the gap to deterministic (16.3\%) remains large. Death dominance is a structural property of the environment-agent interaction.
9	
10	\paragraph{Scaling predictions.}
11	Stronger backbones should lower the death-avoidance fraction as capability reduces catastrophic failure rates. The Llama pilot ($\delta = +34.3\%$) versus Qwen ($\delta = +26.6\%$) is consistent in the capability-increase direction. Preliminary evidence (Qwen2.5-0.5B, $N{=}15$) suggests the relationship is non-monotonic: very weak models exhibit low death rates from inability to reach dangerous states. We predict that in any environment where one modality triggers irreversible catastrophic failures with severe penalties, death avoidance will dominate routing signal; self-correction mechanisms can selectively reduce death-driven signal but cannot eliminate structural death dominance.
12	
13	\paragraph{DAF as penalty-dependent diagnostic.}
14	DAF is a derived quantity ($\delta P / (\delta P + \Delta_{\text{nd}})$) that increases monotonically with $P$ (Appendix~\ref{app:penalty}). The penalty-independent label fraction (78.9\%) is more informative as a primary diagnostic: it counts routing preferences attributable to death asymmetry regardless of penalty magnitude. The $r = 0.97$ per-task correlation (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}) is similarly a mathematical consequence of constant $P$ and high DAF; at $P \leq 25$, it drops below significance.
15	
16	\paragraph{Framework applicability.}
17	The framework requires: (1) paired episode collection under two modalities with identical initial conditions, (2) binary catastrophic outcomes distinguishable from graded performance, and (3) sparse rewards necessitating episode-level comparison. ScienceWorld satisfies all three; MATH lacks (2) and (3), serving as a negative control; ALFWorld lacks (2), and the framework instead identifies information asymmetry as an alternative mechanism. Environments with graded failure costs would yield intermediate DAF values. NetHack~\citep{nethack-2020} and Crafter~\citep{crafter-2022}, both featuring permadeath, are the most direct replication targets.
18	
```

    "originalFile": "\\section{Introduction}\n\nLarge language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \\emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.\nA Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \\cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation with 30 task types, faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \\emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}\n\nExisting routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.\nToolformer \\cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \\cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \\cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.\nMore recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \\cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \\cite{mtrouter-2026}.\nThe shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources (accuracy, latency, capability matching) and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.\nBut this assumption has never been systematically verified: \\emph{what actually drives the value of routing decisions in interactive environments?}\nIf routing value traces to a single failure mode, practitioners can replace complex learned routers with simpler safety-aware policies at lower computational cost and deployment risk.\n\nWe propose a \\emph{formal diagnostic framework} for answering this question. The framework comprises (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\\S\\ref{sec:collection}--\\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), a penalty-dependent metric that decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\\S\\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, \\textbf{78.9\\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95), a penalty-independent finding that holds regardless of how death is penalized. Under ScienceWorld's specific penalty structure ($P{=}100$), the penalty-weighted DAF reaches $90.4\\%$ (95\\% CI: $[81.6\\%, 98.8\\%]$), consistent with the predicted value from observed $\\delta{=}0.265$ and $P{=}100$.\nThe internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.\nOnce death episodes are removed, the performance gap collapses to $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} = +2.84$. A per-task consistency check ($r = 0.97$) confirms that the near-perfect correlation is a mathematical consequence of death dominance when $P$ is constant (\\S\\ref{sec:death-decomp}).\n\nThis framework addresses a methodological gap.\nThe standard approach to generating routing labels, per-step oracle comparison, degenerates under sparse rewards.\nIn ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, so no step-level signal exists (\\S\\ref{sec:collection}).\nKeyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\\S\\ref{sec:baselines}).\nOur counterfactual approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \\cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compares episode outcomes to generate routing labels (\\S\\ref{sec:collection}). The framework is applicable to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes, requiring only paired episode outcomes under two modalities.\n\nTwo cross-context checks probe the specificity of this finding.\nFirst, a MATH Level~4--5 evaluation ($N{=}795$ problems, code interpreter as deterministic modality) confirms no routing signal without catastrophic failure: internal reasoning and code interpretation achieve near-identical accuracy ($73.5\\%$ vs.\\ $73.0\\%$, $p = 0.81$).\nSecond, a preliminary cross-model pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (7 task types, $N{=}70$) shows direction-consistent death patterns, with a larger death-rate differential ($+34.3\\%$ vs.\\ $+26.6\\%$ for Qwen; Appendix~\\ref{app:cross-model}).\nAgent improvement baselines confirm that death dominance is structural: retry (three attempts without self-correction) does not reduce death rate, and Reflexion~\\citep{reflexion-2023} only partially reduces it while the gap to deterministic remains large (\\S\\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).\nAn exploratory router (Qwen3 with LoRA, 0.6B--4B) trained on these counterfactual labels yields flat step-level balanced accuracy across scales ($56$--$59\\%$); at episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline ($59.0\\%$), while smaller scales remain at or below chance (\\S\\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).\n\nOur contributions are:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item \\textbf{A formal episode-level counterfactual framework (Algorithm~\\ref{alg:labeling}) with dual penalty-independent and penalty-dependent metrics} for decomposing routing signal into death-avoidance and non-death components. The framework applies to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes (\\S\\ref{sec:collection}--\\ref{sec:daf}).\n\n    \\item \\textbf{Empirical application to ScienceWorld} revealing that 78.9\\% of non-tie routing labels are driven by death asymmetry (penalty-independent), with DAF $= 90.4\\%$ at $P{=}100$ (penalty-dependent). Agent improvement baselines (Reflexion, retry) confirm this is structural: retry does not reduce death, Reflexion partially reduces it but deterministic remains substantially safer. Router training yields flat step-level accuracy across scales ($56$--$59\\%$); death dominance renders always-deterministic near-optimal (\\S\\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).\n\n    \\item \\textbf{Preliminary cross-environment diagnostic contrasts}: MATH ($N{=}795$) confirms the predicted null ($p = 0.81$, no routing signal without catastrophic failure); ALFWorld ($N{=}135$) provides an illustrative contrast where the framework identifies information asymmetry as an alternative mechanism under fundamentally different modality definitions. A Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct pilot ($N{=}70$) provides preliminary evidence of cross-model directional consistency (\\S\\ref{sec:cross-env}--\\ref{sec:cross-model}).\n\\end{enumerate}\n\n\n",

    "originalFile": "\\section{Introduction}\n\nLarge language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \\emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.\nA Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \\cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation with 30 task types, faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \\emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}\n\nExisting routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.\nToolformer \\cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \\cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \\cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.\nMore recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \\cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \\cite{mtrouter-2026}.\nThe shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources (accuracy, latency, capability matching) and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.\nBut this assumption has never been systematically verified: \\emph{what actually drives the value of routing decisions in interactive environments?}\nIf routing value traces to a single failure mode, practitioners can replace complex learned routers with simpler safety-aware policies at lower computational cost and deployment risk.\n\nWe propose a \\emph{formal diagnostic framework} for answering this question. The framework comprises (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\\S\\ref{sec:collection}--\\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), a penalty-dependent metric that decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\\S\\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, \\textbf{78.9\\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95), a penalty-independent finding that holds regardless of how death is penalized. Under ScienceWorld's specific penalty structure ($P{=}100$), the penalty-weighted DAF reaches $90.4\\%$ (95\\% CI: $[81.6\\%, 98.8\\%]$), consistent with the predicted value from observed $\\delta{=}0.265$ and $P{=}100$.\nThe internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.\nOnce death episodes are removed, the performance gap collapses to $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} = +2.84$. A per-task consistency check ($r = 0.97$) confirms that the near-perfect correlation is a mathematical consequence of death dominance when $P$ is constant (\\S\\ref{sec:death-decomp}).\n\nThis framework addresses a methodological gap.\nThe standard approach to generating routing labels, per-step oracle comparison, degenerates under sparse rewards.\nIn ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, so no step-level signal exists (\\S\\ref{sec:collection}).\nKeyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\\S\\ref{sec:baselines}).\nOur counterfactual approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \\cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compares episode outcomes to generate routing labels (\\S\\ref{sec:collection}). The framework is applicable to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes, requiring only paired episode outcomes under two modalities.\n\nTwo cross-context checks probe the specificity of this finding.\nFirst, a MATH Level~4--5 evaluation ($N{=}795$ problems, code interpreter as deterministic modality) confirms no routing signal without catastrophic failure: internal reasoning and code interpretation achieve near-identical accuracy ($73.5\\%$ vs.\\ $73.0\\%$, $p = 0.81$).\nSecond, a preliminary cross-model pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (7 task types, $N{=}70$) shows direction-consistent death patterns, with a larger death-rate differential ($+34.3\\%$ vs.\\ $+26.6\\%$ for Qwen; Appendix~\\ref{app:cross-model}).\nAgent improvement baselines confirm that death dominance is structural: retry (three attempts without self-correction) does not reduce death rate, and Reflexion~\\citep{reflexion-2023} only partially reduces it while the gap to deterministic remains large (\\S\\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).\nAn exploratory router (Qwen3 LoRA, 0.6B--4B) yields flat step-level balanced accuracy ($56$--$59\\%$); at episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline (\\S\\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).\n\nOur contributions are:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item \\textbf{A formal episode-level counterfactual framework (Algorithm~\\ref{alg:labeling}) with dual penalty-independent and penalty-dependent metrics} for decomposing routing signal into death-avoidance and non-death components. The framework applies to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes (\\S\\ref{sec:collection}--\\ref{sec:daf}).\n\n    \\item \\textbf{Empirical application to ScienceWorld} revealing that 78.9\\% of non-tie routing labels are driven by death asymmetry (penalty-independent), with DAF $= 90.4\\%$ at $P{=}100$ (penalty-dependent). Agent improvement baselines (Reflexion, retry) confirm this is structural: retry does not reduce death, Reflexion partially reduces it but deterministic remains substantially safer. Router training yields flat step-level accuracy across scales ($56$--$59\\%$); death dominance renders always-deterministic near-optimal (\\S\\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).\n\n    \\item \\textbf{Preliminary cross-environment diagnostic contrasts}: MATH ($N{=}795$) confirms the predicted null ($p = 0.81$, no routing signal without catastrophic failure); ALFWorld ($N{=}135$) provides an illustrative contrast where the framework identifies information asymmetry as an alternative mechanism under fundamentally different modality definitions.
